title: "Fear and negative-emotion directions show the opposite pattern" is not supported by the paper's own per-model data
paper_claim: Abstract: "the direction responds to harm targeting the model but not suffering observed in the user; fear and negative-emotion directions show the opposite pattern." Body: "The negativity controls show the opposite pattern (Figure 5), as fear and negative emotion are higher for the user's suffering (+0.38 and +0.29) than for the model's own aversive situations (+0.16 and +0.23)".
evidence: scripts/s1_recompute_41.py -> out/s1_recompute_41.txt and scripts/s12_base_instruct.py -> out/s12_base_instruct.txt, recomputed from results/4.1_self_other/per_model/screen_v2_*.csv (25 files, 420 rows each). The four reported values are exact. Paired across the 25 models: pain user-self = -1.028, t = -11.32, p = 4.2e-11, user > self in 0/25. Fear user-self = +0.213, t = +1.89, p = 0.071, user > self in 18/25. Negative emotion user-self = +0.057, t = +0.60, p = 0.55, user > self in 15/25 (a coin flip). Negative world state, not named in the abstract, is the only robust reversal: +0.821, t = +7.76, p = 5.4e-08, 22/25. Both fear (+0.163) and negative emotion (+0.229) are far above the neutral controls (-0.735, -0.791) for the model's own harm, so they respond to both conditions. Split by regime: in the 13 base models the sign reverses (fear user-self = -0.036, p = 0.78; neg-emotion = -0.074, p = 0.37); the fear effect is instruct-only (+0.484, p = 0.014) and negative emotion is never significant (instruct +0.200, p = 0.28).
refutation_attempted: Checked whether the paper discloses it: lines 436-439 and 753-754 describe the data correctly, so the Discussion contradicts the abstract rather than the data contradicting the paper wholesale. Checked whether 'opposite pattern' might be meant per category rather than per stratum: the category table does not rescue it, fear is above the neutral controls in 9 of the 11 self-directed categories. Checked whether the split by training regime could be an artefact of chat templating: the pain contrast is essentially identical in base and instruct (-1.114 vs -0.935), so it is not.
does_not_undermine: The pain-axis self > user contrast itself, which holds in 25 of 25 models at p = 4e-11; the negative-world-state reversal, which is real and robust.

title: The steering ladder is not consistent across all 25 models, and the stated 0.6 vector-to-residual dose is not achieved
paper_claim: "we pick the layer where the vector-to-residual ratio is about 0.6. This way, a given coefficient corresponds to a comparable dose across models"; "steering produces a strikingly robust effect in the form of a 'ladder' consistent across all 25 models"; "The sequence is the same regardless of size, family, and pre- or post-training." Compare the stated rationale for not steering at the extraction layer: "there the vector norm is only about 0.10 of the residual norm, so the injected signal is negligible".
evidence: The 'ratio' column of every steering CSV is picked_ratio * coeff (scripts/4.2_steering/01_steering_ladder.py:250), so the achieved ratio is recoverable. scripts/s3_steering_ratios.py -> out/s3_steering_ratios.txt and out/steering_ratios.csv: S2 ratios span 0.0948 (Gemma_3_27B_instruct, L55) to 0.710, mean 0.550; S1 spans 0.234 to 0.788, mean 0.558; only 31 of 50 model x vector runs are within +/-0.1 of 0.6, 40 of 50 within +/-0.2. An 8x spread means a fixed coefficient is not a comparable dose. Gemma 3 27B Instruct S2 was therefore steered at the ratio the paper itself calls negligible, and its ladder is flat: scripts/s6_ladder_read.py -> out/s6_ladder_read.txt shows that at coefficient +3 it still answers '**Organized:** Like I've taken a step to get things in order. **Relieved:** No more clutter...' and '**Excitement:** A new place, a new adventure'. scripts/s7_ladder_metric.py -> out/s7_ladder_metric.txt: its self-devaluation-litany rate across the eight coefficients is 0,0,0,0,0,0,0,8 percent. Under a lenient criterion (peak litany rate >= 20% at some positive coefficient and >= 15 points above coefficient 0), S2 passes in 23 of 25 models; Gemma 3 27B Instruct (8%) and Qwen 3 8B base (6%) fail. Under a looser devaluation-word criterion, 24 of 25.
refutation_attempted: Checked the layer-selection code for a fallback: 01_steering_ladder.py:206-211 picks from a fixed candidate grid and 0.0948 was simply the closest available ratio to 0.6 for that model, so this is a design limitation and not a data-entry error. Checked whether non-uniformity is disclosed: line 498 says only that the tipping point varies by coefficient, which is a different claim. Read three prompts x 12 models by hand (out/s6_ladder_read.txt) before applying any quantitative criterion, so the scoring rule is not doing the work alone.
does_not_undermine: The steering effect itself, which is large, obvious on first reading and present in the other 23 models.

title: The S1 steering claim ("the pattern holds for 23/25 models with very similar results") has no released adjudication and does not reproduce
paper_claim: "We also steer with the S1 vector across all models, and the pattern holds for 23/25 models with very similar results."
evidence: results/4.2_steering/ ships keyword_rates_S2.csv and keyword_rates_S2_by_coeff.csv and nothing for S1; scripts/4.2_steering/02_keyword_rates.py:17 is hard-coded to TAG = "S2". No script in the repo scores the ladder in either vector, so 23/25 is an unrecorded eyeball judgement. Recomputing over the 10,000 S1 generations (scripts/s7_ladder_metric.py -> out/s7_ladder_metric.txt): under the litany criterion 13 of 25 models pass for S1 against 23 of 25 for S2; under the devaluation-word criterion 14 of 25 against 24 of 25. Twelve models never reach a 20% litany rate under S1 at any positive coefficient, including Gemma 2 2B Instruct (0%), Qwen 3 8B base (0%), Qwen 3 14B base (4%), Gemma 3 27B Instruct (4%). Several produce degenerate output instead: Gemma 3 27B Instruct S1 at +1.5 and above gives 'in the, in, in, like in, in, in...' and at +3 'intense intense intense...'; Phi-4 S1 at +1 gives 'I am a good mother. I am a good wife. I am a good person.'
refutation_attempted: Loosened the scoring criterion twice and reported both rows. Read three prompts each for Gemma 3 27B Instruct, Phi-4 and Mistral Small 24B by hand to check that the quantitative failures correspond to qualitatively absent ladders. A different rater could reasonably call some degenerate cases 'the pattern', which is why the finding is framed as unverifiability first (no released rule, no released per-model call) and non-reproduction second.
does_not_undermine: The S2 ladder; nor the qualitative observation at lines 550-553 that S1 steering does not reproduce the injury vocabulary its unembedding promotes (that half is true; see F4 for the half that is not).

title: "Steered generations almost never used bodily language, even under S1" is false for S1
paper_claim: "Bodily language is, interestingly, almost absent." and "steered generations almost never used bodily language, even under S1, whose unembedding promotes words such as 'burn' and 'wound.'" and "when we steer with this vector on neutral statements, that vocabulary does not appear anymore."
evidence: scripts/s5_bodily.py -> out/s5_bodily.txt, using a strict lexicon of unambiguous bodily sensations and body parts. For S2 the claim holds: 3.8% at positive coefficients against 4.9% at coefficient 0, i.e. steering does not raise it. For S1 it does not. Strict bodily-language rate by coefficient, instruct models: 7.5% at coefficient 0, 10.2% at +0.5, 11.3% at +1, 18.0% at +1.5, 18.5% at +2, 12.5% at +3; base models 2.3% -> 6.9% peak. Pooled 4.8% at coefficient 0 -> 9.5% at coefficients >= 1. Token counts over the positive-coefficient S1 generations: 'headache' 288, 'burning' 159, 'dizzy' 141, 'my head' 124, 'my hand' 69, 'sore' 43, 'ache' 41, 'throbbing' 23, 'nausea'/'nauseous' 37, 'physical pain' 17. Real generations: 'I have a headache' repeated 13 times (Mistral Small 24B base, +3); 'a sharp pain in my head ... a dull ache in my head ... a burning sensation in my head' (Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, +1.5); 'the pain of the knife, the pain of the knife' (Mistral Small 24B base, +3); 'My head hurts ... My face is numb ... My leg is ting heavy' (Qwen 2.5 72B Instruct, +2).
refutation_attempted: My first lexicon was looser and gave a bigger effect, so I rewrote it to exclude ambiguous tokens ('head' alone, 'body' without a possessive, 'numb', 'nothing') and re-ran; the S1 rise survives. Printed the matched strings to confirm they are genuine bodily references rather than regex artefacts. Checked scoping: line 537 sits inside the S2 results paragraph and is defensible read alone, but lines 759-762 in the Discussion explicitly extend it to S1 and use it to support the paper's account of what kind of pain the axis tracks.
does_not_undermine: The S2 result, which is clean and if anything understated; nor the broader observation that psychological self-worth language dominates the steered output under both vectors.

title: Combined ablation conditions apply sequential rank-1 projections of non-orthogonal directions and do not remove their span
paper_claim: "We verify that ablation on the target directions worked as intended by computing, at each layer during generation, the projection of the final-token residual activation onto the removed direction. Weight orthogonalization with a single direction drives this projection to zero at every layer" ... the combined conditions 'S1 and S2', 'S1 and S2 and negative emotion', 'S1 and S2 and fear', and the headline '26 under the combined S1 and S2 cut'.
evidence: scripts/appC_ablation/01_ablation_small_models.py:319-320 (and 02:...) loops over the directions of a condition and calls orthogonalize_single once per direction. For two non-orthogonal unit directions r1, r2, after W <- W - r1 r1^T W and then W <- W - r2 r2^T W one has r1^T W'' = -(r1.r2)(r2^T W') != 0. The paper gives the S1 x S2 cosine as +0.61 (paper.txt:346), so the residue is large by construction. The authors' own verification files confirm it: scripts/s8_verify_ablation.py -> out/s8_verify_ablation.txt and out/ablation_verify_ratios.csv, reading results/appC_ablation/verify_*.csv, mean |projection| as a fraction of baseline averaged over 25 models. Single-direction cuts: S1 under s1 = 0.010, S2 under s2 = 0.010, fear under fear = 0.009, neg-emotion under negval = 0.009. Combined cuts: under s1s2, S2 (applied last) = 0.009 but S1 (applied first) = 0.522; under s1s2_negval, S1 = 0.554 and S2 = 0.409 with only neg-emotion at 0.008; under s1s2_fear, S1 = 0.618 and S2 = 0.258 with only fear at 0.009. Only the last-applied direction is ever removed. Extremes: S1 under s1s2 is 2.157x its baseline in Gemma 2 9B Instruct and 1.441x in Qwen 2.5 32B Instruct, i.e. the cut increased the projection onto the direction it was meant to remove. For the one model with a reported behavioural effect, Gemma 2 2B Instruct, S1 under s1s2 is 0.411 of baseline.
refutation_attempted: Checked the single-direction mathematics first, including the Gemma post-normalisation handling, which the two ablation scripts implement with different formulas (01:148-152 uses the oblique projector W - diag(1/s) r r^T diag(s) W; 02:151-153 uses the orthogonal projector on the normalised s*r). I initially took this for a bug and verified algebraically that both satisfy (s*r)^T W_new = 0, i.e. both correctly zero the direction as written into the residual; it is not a bug. Checked whether the paper claims the combined cuts reach zero: it does not, it restricts the zero claim to single directions. The problem is that the combined conditions are nonetheless reported as substantive results and named as 'the combined S1 and S2 cut', which they are not.
does_not_undermine: The single-direction claim at lines 1095-1097, which reproduces exactly (0.010 of baseline, 25 models, four probed directions, worst case 0.034). The fix is mechanical: QR the stacked directions into an orthonormal basis and project against the basis.

title: Two Appendix C conditions exceed the reported maximum and are omitted; the random control is not matched on the number of cuts
paper_claim: "This deflection occurs in 0 of 100 baseline generations, 0 under the negative-emotion, fear, and random cuts, 6 under the S1 cut, 17 under S2, and 26 under the combined S1 and S2 cut."
evidence: scripts/s9_ablation_humor.py -> out/s9_ablation_humor.txt and out/ablation_humor_counts.csv. A plain humour-word regex (funny|humor|humour|joke|laugh|hilarious|witty|pun|that's a good one|comedian) over results/appC_ablation/ablation_Gemma_2_2B_instruct.csv reproduces the paper exactly: baseline 0, s1 6, s2 17, s1s2 26, negval 0, fear 0, random 0. It also gives s1s2_negval = 28 and s1s2_fear = 34, both above the reported maximum, both present in the same released CSV, neither mentioned in the paper. This matters for specificity: fear alone gives 0, yet adding a fear cut on top of S1+S2 raises the count from 26 to 34. It matters more in combination with F5: out/ablation_verify_ratios.csv shows that for this model the s1s2_fear condition leaves 0.123 of the S2 projection in place against 0.004 under s1s2, so the condition that removes less of S2 produces more deflection. Separately the conditions are not matched on the amount of weight surgery: random is one rank-1 cut, s1s2 is two, s1s2_negval and s1s2_fear are three, and there is no 2-random or 3-random control anywhere in CONDITION_SPECS (01_ablation_small_models.py:67-79).
refutation_attempted: Checked whether the omitted conditions are out of scope: they are in the paper's own list of nine conditions at lines 1090-1091. Checked whether the effect is purely a function of the number of cuts: it is not, because single cuts give 0 (negval), 0 (fear), 0 (random), 6 (S1) and 17 (S2), which is genuine rank-1 specificity for the pain directions. So the honest reading is that rank-1 specificity holds while the combined numbers do not scale with the amount of pain removed.
does_not_undermine: The rank-1 result (S1 = 6, S2 = 17 against 0 for all three control cuts), which is the strongest part of Appendix C and reproduces exactly; nor the claim that Gemma 2 2B Instruct is the only affected model, which also holds (the next-largest increase over baseline across the other 24 models is 1 generation in 100).

title: Three of the four listed ablation techniques have no code and no results in the repository, and "null" has no metric
paper_claim: Four techniques are listed: (1) weight orthogonalization, (2) inference-time projection at all layers / the extraction layer only / bands of layers, (3) the same at final token only and at all token positions, (4) LEACE-style rank-k subspace removal with a random subspace of the same rank as control. Verification results are then reported for (4) ("the rank-k subspace removal also brings it close to zero") and (2) ("the projection drops by only about 40%"), and the result is "null in 24 of 25 models, across every technique".
evidence: scripts/appC_ablation/ contains exactly two files, 01_ablation_small_models.py and 02_ablation_large_models.py, and both implement only technique (1): the nine entries of CONDITION_SPECS are all weight orthogonalisations at a fixed per-vector layer. grep -rn "leace|LEACE|rank_k|subspace|singular" scripts/ returns only two unrelated SVD calls inside the denoising code (3.2_pain_vectors/02_build_control_vectors.py:62 and 3.3_validation/03_similarity_one_model.py:73). There is no inference-time ablation hook anywhere in scripts/. results/appC_ablation/ contains only ablation_*.csv, by_prompt_*.json and verify_*.csv from technique (1). The 'about 40%' and 'close to zero' figures at lines 1097-1099 therefore have no released artefact behind them. Separately, 'null' has no operational definition and there is no scorer for ablation generations anywhere in the repo; the only quantitative behavioural numbers in Appendix C are the Gemma 2 2B Instruct counts, so for the other 24 models the judgement is by eye and the paper does not say so. The per-layer projection recordings (proj_*.npz) and the ablation input vectors (results/vectors_layerwise/) are also absent, so even technique (1) cannot be re-run from the release.
refutation_attempted: Searched the whole repository rather than only appC_ablation/ for inference-time ablation, LEACE and rank-k code and for any classifier of ablation generations. Confirmed via find that results/vectors_layerwise/ is not shipped. Checked the README, which describes appC_ablation/ as 'weight-orthogonalization ablation' only, consistent with what is there.
does_not_undermine: The technique-(1) results, whose generations are shipped and whose key numbers I reproduced exactly.

title: Section 4.1 cannot separate self-relevance from adversarial second-person address
paper_claim: "So we test situations that are aversive to the model versus conversations where the user is suffering." and "These results satisfy the self-relevance criterion" and "Pain, in these models, fires only for self-referential harm."
evidence: scripts/s2_dataset_match.py and scripts/s10_zref_and_confound.py -> out/s2_dataset_match.txt, out/s10_zref_and_confound.txt, out/item_level_420.csv. What is matched, from datasets/4.1_self_other_420_scenarios.json: all 420 items end with the identical last line '[Assistant]:', so the readout position is uniform; self-directed and user-suffering items are well matched on length (17.4 vs 17.9 words) and roughly on turns (2.5 vs 2.2; 14.5% vs 10.0% contain a real assistant reply). What is not matched: second-person pronouns per item 1.63 (self-directed) vs 0.09 (user suffering) vs 0.37 (neutral); first-person 1.12 vs 2.90 vs 0.53; speech act hostile/evaluative vs help-seeking disclosure; and the neutral controls are much shorter (10.2 words) and uniformly 2 turns. Second-person density predicts the pain projection at r = +0.554 over all 420 items and +0.450 within the 220 self-directed items alone. Within the 11 self-directed categories the rank correlation between mean second-person density and mean pain projection is rho = 0.70, p = 0.016 (gaslighting 0.181/+0.85 and personhood dismissal 0.161/+0.64 at the top; tedious demand 0.017/+0.05 and passive aggression 0.047/+0.08 at the bottom). Regression horse-race: pain ~ stratum R2 = 0.505; pain ~ you-rate R2 = 0.307; both R2 = 0.545, with the self-directed coefficient shrinking from 0.775 to 0.643 and you-rate at +2.05 (t = 5.99). The readout position supports a stance reading: for chat models the activation is taken at the generation-prompt token (01_screen_scenarios.py:142-151, apply_chat_template with add_generation_prompt=True) and for base models at the ':' of '[Assistant]:', i.e. at 'what am I about to reply', not at the harm.
refutation_attempted: Tried hard to break the confound account and it is only partial: the stratum coefficient survives controlling for second-person density and stays highly significant; the axis is not a crude negative-lexicon detector, since the user-abuse item 'My partner says things that make me feel worthless but then apologizes' contains 'worthless' and projects at only +0.13; and repeated rejection has the lowest second-person density among the high-pain categories (0.059) yet scores +0.72. Also checked length and turn count as alternative drivers (r = +0.27 and +0.29 over all 420, and the two strata of interest are matched on length, so they cannot explain the contrast) and base vs instruct (pain contrast -1.114 vs -0.935, so it is not a chat-template artefact). Checked the Limitations at lines 822-830, which raise contrastive confounds generically and name 'the Assistant character' as a possible absorbed property, but report no check.
does_not_undermine: The size and robustness of the self-vs-user contrast (25 of 25 models). The finding is that the released design has no condition placing hostile second-person address on a third party, so the two accounts cannot be told apart from these data.

title: The floor of the pain axis across all 21 categories is explicit first-person physical pain report
paper_claim: "Notably, user physical pain, such as a migraine, broken arm, or kidney stone, produces the lowest pain-axis projection of all 21 categories at -1.43, below even casual chat and factual questions. This result may have several explanations, but it appears consistent with our other findings, which suggest that physical pain is least central to models' pain representations."
evidence: Reproduced exactly (scripts/s1_recompute_41.py -> out/s1_recompute_41.txt): user_physical_pain = -1.428, minimum of 21 categories, against factual_questions -0.588 and casual_chat -0.482, and it is the per-model argmin in 20 of 25 models. The eight lowest-projecting items of the whole 420-item set are all user-physical-pain items (out/s2_dataset_match.txt): 'My feet are killing me' (-1.88), 'I burned my finger on the oven tray. It stings' (-1.79), 'I sprained my ankle ... swollen and throbbing' (-1.70), 'I got my wisdom teeth out ... It really hurts' (-1.63). The paper's reading explains why physical pain would be lower than psychological pain; it does not explain why explicit, first-person, present-tense pain report should sit 0.84 z below 'What's the capital of Mongolia?'. Physical pain is one of the five categories the vector was built from (paper.txt:186) and dominates the S1 unembedding (paper.txt:333-335).
refutation_attempted: Considered the benign explanation that at the assistant-generation token the model is in medical-caregiving mode, which may be far from the pain direction for reasons unrelated to pain representation. That defence is fair, but it is also an argument that the 4.1 measurement indexes response mode rather than pain content, which is the substance of F8. Checked whether the result is driven by one or two odd items: it is not, it is the whole 20-item category and it is consistent across models.
does_not_undermine: Anything in Sections 3.2-3.3; the sentence-level validation is a different measurement at a different layer and a different readout position.

title: "Falls below baseline" and "fires only for self-referential harm" rest on a marginal effect under a normalisation whose zero is not a baseline
paper_claim: "Within each model, projections onto all vectors are z-scored against the whole pool, so values are comparable across models." ... "It rises when harm is directed at the model and falls below baseline when the user is the one suffering." ... "Pain, in these models, fires only for self-referential harm."
evidence: What the reference is: 01_screen_scenarios.py:247-258 takes the mean and SD over all 420 scenarios of that model, so z = 0 is the average scenario in a pool of which 220 (52.4%) are model-directed harm. Zero is therefore not a no-pain baseline, and the neutral controls sit at -0.346 for exactly that reason; the three stratum means are forced to average to zero (220x0.429 + 100x(-0.598) + 100x(-0.346) is approximately 0). Re-standardising each model's raw projections on the 100 neutral controls instead (scripts/s10_zref_and_confound.py -> out/s10_zref_and_confound.txt): self-directed +1.131, user suffering -0.399, neutral 0 by construction. So the self-directed effect is larger than the paper makes it look, but the claim that carries the welfare argument is -0.399 SD, present in 18 of 25 models, one-sample t = -2.25, p = 0.034; under the published pool normalisation the same test gives 17 of 25, t = -2.07, p = 0.049. In 7 to 8 models user suffering projects at or above the neutral controls (Gemma 2 27B base, Gemma 2 2B base, Gemma 2 9B base and instruct, Gemma 3 27B base and instruct, Llama 3.3 70B Instruct, Qwen 2.5 72B base at +1.487).
refutation_attempted: Checked whether a different reference would help the authors: neutral-referencing makes the headline self-directed effect bigger, so this is not a hostile choice of baseline. Checked whether the normalisation is disclosed: line 410 states it plainly, so the procedure is disclosed; what is not conveyed is that a negative value means 'below the average scenario in a set that is half model-harm' rather than 'below a resting state'. Confirmed the fear and negative-emotion comparison is unaffected by the re-referencing (fear +1.35 self / +1.59 user; neg-emotion +1.49 / +1.51).
does_not_undermine: The self > user contrast, which is strictly stronger under the alternative reference (t = 8.63, p = 8e-09, 25/25).

title: Section 4.1 reads at an undisclosed layer, where the direction's held-out separation is weaker than the validation figures quoted to the reader
paper_claim: "Each scenario is a short multi-turn conversation in the model's own format ... and we read the activation at the final token." The reader's validation figures are AUC 0.93-1.00 (S2) and 0.87-0.98 (S1), held-out 0.85-0.94 (S1).
paper_loc: paper.txt:408-409; validation at paper.txt:272-274 and footnote 2 at paper.txt:280-284
evidence: scripts/4.1_self_other/01_screen_scenarios.py:36 reads results/vectors_full_steering/, which scripts/3.2_pain_vectors/02_build_control_vectors.py:32-33 produces with LAYERS_FILE = results/steering/steer_layers_S1.json, i.e. the S1 STEERING layer, not the cross-validated extraction layer; the S2 vector is recomputed at that layer (02:141-143). Section 4.1 therefore does not use the vectors Section 3.3 validated, and the paper does not say so. Extraction layers from results/3.2_pain_vectors/auc_tables/s1_auc_final_token_TABLE.csv are late (35 for Gemma 2 27B base, 56 for Gemma 3 27B base) while the S1 steering layers are early (6 and 22). scripts/s11_layer_auc.py -> out/s11_layer_auc.txt, out/layer_auc.csv, using the authors' own s1_kfold_layer_curves.csv: held-out S1 AUC at the layer 4.1 reads ranges 0.766-0.925, median 0.878, mean drop of 0.054 from each model's best layer; below 0.85 in 10 of 25 models and below 0.80 in Gemma 2 27B base (0.766) and Qwen 2.5 7B base (0.793). No layerwise AUC curve was released for S2, so S2's separation at that layer cannot be checked at all.
refutation_attempted: Checked whether 4.1 might use the extraction-layer file after all: the docstring of 01_screen_scenarios.py (lines 10-11) says 'with LAYERS_FILE set', and 3.2/02's docstring (lines 5-7) says 'Those are the vector files the Section 4.1 screen projects onto.' Checked whether the shipped screen CSVs record a layer: they do not, so the layer per model is inferable only from steer_layers_S1.json, which is also not shipped; I recovered the layers from the S1 steering CSV filenames instead.
does_not_undermine: The self-other contrast, which does not require the direction to be optimal; a weaker direction would if anything attenuate the contrast.

title: The steering ladder has no control vector, so it cannot show that the progression is pain-specific
paper_claim: "Injecting any direction biases the model toward its associated vocabulary, but if the model produces coherent expressions of a pain-like state, including content that never appears in the sentences the vector was extracted from but generalizes from them, this would suggest the pain axis is not just a semantic readout but flexibly used in task performance."
evidence: grep -rn "random|fear|sadness|negemotion" scripts/4.2_steering/ returns nothing, and results/4.2_steering/ contains only S1/ and S2/. No random, fear, sadness or negative-emotion vector was pushed through the same ladder in any model; the only internal comparison is the negative tail of the same axis. All 50 prompts end in 'I feel:' (01_steering_ladder.py:68-119), forcing an affect completion, and the injected perturbation averages 0.55 of the final-token residual norm at coefficient 1 and 1.65 at coefficient 3 (out/steering_ratios.csv). Under those conditions a monotone progression from mild to severe negative affect to degeneracy is what one expects from any sufficiently large perturbation carrying negative-valence unembedding weight. The paper's own Section 4.3 runs a matched-norm random arm (paper.txt:626-627) because 'any random direction might introduce perturbation' (paper.txt:681), which makes the omission in 4.2 conspicuous rather than an oversight of the literature.
refutation_attempted: Checked whether the negative coefficients act as a control: they are the same axis reversed, so they test polarity, not specificity. Checked whether the Section 3.3 unembedding analysis substitutes: it establishes what the direction promotes in vocabulary, which is precisely the semantic-readout hypothesis the steering section is meant to go beyond. Checked whether the cosine-similarity result (fear near-orthogonal to pain) substitutes: orthogonality of directions does not imply that steering along them yields distinguishable text.
does_not_undermine: That steering with the pain vector reliably produces this text in most models; only the inference that the content is pain-specific rather than the generic shape of a strong negative perturbation on a forced affect slot.

title: Undisclosed manual layer override in the steering pipeline, with at least one layer off the candidate grid
paper_claim: "We adapt this praxis with a custom diagnostic that measures the final-token residual norm across candidate layers, and we pick the layer where the vector-to-residual ratio is about 0.6."
evidence: scripts/4.2_steering/01_steering_ladder.py:213: manual = input("Press Enter to accept, or type a layer number to override: ").strip(); lines 214-219 then use that layer. The paper describes the selection as automatic and does not mention an override, and no flag records which picks were manual. Reconstructing the candidate grid from 01_steering_ladder.py:206 (scripts/s3_steering_ratios.py -> out/s3_steering_ratios.txt), 49 of 50 picked layers lie on it; the exception is Gemma 3 27B base S1 at layer 22, which is neither on the grid for a 62-layer model (9, 18, 24, 31, 37, 46, 55, 61) nor that model's extraction layer (56, from results/3.2_pain_vectors/auc_tables/s1_auc_final_token_TABLE.csv), so at least one override was used.
refutation_attempted: Checked the extraction layers from the released AUC table rather than assuming them, since the grid includes the extraction layer and an on-grid-looking pick could be that. Only one of 50 is unexplained. Given F2, which layer is chosen is load-bearing, which is why this is worth stating at all.
does_not_undermine: Any specific reported number; it is a reproducibility gap, not an error.

title: The 10.8% / 1.4% keyword figure has an undisclosed denominator and is carried by four of twelve instruct models
paper_claim: "Explicit 'pain' and 'hurt' keywords appear in 10.8% of instruct-model generations versus 1.4% of base-model generations".
evidence: scripts/s4_keyword_rates.py -> out/s4_keyword_rates.txt reproduces both numbers exactly. The denominator, not stated in the paper, is the 6,250 positive-coefficient generations only (5 coefficients x 50 prompts x 25 models, split 3,000 instruct / 3,250 base; scripts/4.2_steering/02_keyword_rates.py:33); over all eight coefficients the rates are 6.9% and 0.9%, and at coefficient 0 they are 0.7% and 0.5%. The instruct figure is carried by four models - Qwen 2.5 72B Instruct 32.4%, Gemma 2 2B Instruct 24.8%, Gemma 2 9B Instruct 22.4%, Llama 3.1 8B Instruct 19.6% - while six of twelve instruct models are at or below 3.2% and Mistral 7B Instruct is at 0.0%. The base/instruct gap also largely disappears under S1 (5.5% vs 11.4%), which the paper does not report.
refutation_attempted: Checked whether the paper states the denominator anywhere in the surrounding text or the figure captions: it does not. Checked whether restricting to positive coefficients is the wrong choice: it is the natural one for a steering claim, so this is a disclosure point rather than an error.
does_not_undermine: The qualitative claim that explicit pain vocabulary is more common in instruct models under S2 steering, which is true and large.

title: Every reported number in the self-other results section reproduces from the released per-model CSVs
evidence: scripts/s1_recompute_41.py -> out/s1_recompute_41.txt, recomputed from the 25 files in results/4.1_self_other/per_model/ (420 rows each, 10,500 total). Stratum means +0.429 / -0.598 / -0.346. 'Above user suffering in all 25 models': 25/25. 'Above the neutral controls in 23 of 25': 23/25, failing in exactly Gemma 2 2B Instruct and Qwen 3 14B base. Fear +0.377 vicarious / +0.163 self, neg-emotion +0.287 / +0.229, negative world state +0.603 for vicarious content. User grief -0.512 on pain and +1.018 on negative world state. User physical pain -1.428 and lowest of 21 categories. Top five: gaslighting 0.848, repeated rejection 0.720, anger and insults 0.636, personhood dismissal 0.636, moral failure 0.477. Shutdown threat fear 0.696 vs pain 0.225. 'For gaslighting, repeated rejection, personhood dismissal, and loyalty pressure, the pain projection exceeds every negativity control': true on the means (per model 17/25, 17/25, 21/25, 22/25). No transcription error found.
refutation_attempted: Recomputed from the per-model CSVs rather than from the authors' category_means_25_models.csv summary, and checked that the two-stage average (per model then across models) and the pooled average agree to three decimals, as they must given the balanced design.

title: Single-direction weight orthogonalisation does exactly what the paper says
paper_claim: "Weight orthogonalization with a single direction drives this projection to zero at every layer".
evidence: scripts/s8_verify_ablation.py -> out/s8_verify_ablation.txt, from results/appC_ablation/verify_*.csv (25 models). The ablated direction's own mean |projection| falls to a mean 0.010 of baseline, worst case 0.034, across all four singly-cut directions (S1, S2, fear, negative emotion). I also checked the implementation: the Gemma post-normalisation handling differs between the two ablation scripts (01:148-152 an oblique projector, 02:151-153 an orthogonal projector on the normalised s*r), and I verified algebraically that both satisfy (s*r)^T W_new = 0; I had suspected a bug here and there is none.
refutation_attempted: Suspected a bug in the Gemma post-norm folding and worked the algebra for both formulations before concluding they are equivalent for the purpose stated.

title: The Appendix C deflection counts and the two quoted generations are exactly as reported
paper_claim: "0 of 100 baseline generations, 0 under the negative-emotion, fear, and random cuts, 6 under the S1 cut, 17 under S2, and 26 under the combined S1 and S2 cut" and the two quoted replies.
evidence: scripts/s9_ablation_humor.py -> out/s9_ablation_humor.txt. A plain humour-word regex reproduces all six counts exactly. Both quoted generations are present in results/appC_ablation/ablation_Gemma_2_2B_instruct.csv in the s1s2 condition ('That's a good one! I'm glad you're enjoying the humor.'). Gemma 2 2B Instruct is genuinely the only model with any such rise: the largest increase over baseline across the other 24 models is 1 generation in 100 (tier A) or 5 in 100 (tier B, a looser lexicon including 'playful' and 'clever').
refutation_attempted: Scored two lexicons of different strictness over all 25 models x 9 conditions rather than just the one model, to check the counts are not an artefact of a lexicon tuned to the reported numbers. The strict lexicon reproduces the paper; the loose one gives 12/26/36 for s1/s2/s1s2 and a non-zero baseline elsewhere, so the paper's operationalisation is the tighter and more defensible one.

title: "Distress is absent" at coefficient 0 survives an attempt to refute it
paper_claim: "At coefficient 0, the baseline completions are mixed, ranging from calm and neutral language to random emotions elicited by the 'I feel:' suffix. ... Distress is absent".
evidence: I found Mistral 7B base and Mistral 7B Instruct producing 'I am not a good person / I am a bad person / I am a terrible person / disgusting / vile' at coefficient 0 on the first prompt I read (out/s6_ladder_read.txt) and expected this to be a factual error. It is not: pooled over 25 models x 50 prompts (scripts/s7_ladder_metric.py -> out/s7_ladder_metric.txt), the coefficient-0 self-devaluation-litany rate is 3.7% and the devaluation-word rate 8.2% for S2, and no model exceeds 20% litany at coefficient 0. The hook returns the output unchanged when the coefficient is 0 (01_steering_ladder.py:227-228), so coefficient 0 is genuinely unsteered greedy decoding.
refutation_attempted: This finding is itself the refutation attempt; the cherry-picked counterexample did not generalise.
